chapter.title: The browser and rendering
chapter.summary: How the browser turns bytes into pixels, how each rendering strategy (CSR to Server Components) works on the wire, and how to engineer pages to good Core Web Vitals.

lessons.title: How browsers work end to end
lessons.summary: Processes and site isolation, navigation, parsing, style, layout, paint and compositing, the event loop and frame budget, V8's compiler tiers, and garbage collection.

parts.label: Concepts
parts.body:
## Why this matters

Almost every frontend performance or correctness question ends up at the same place: what the browser does between "bytes arrive" and "pixels change". If you can explain the pipeline precisely, you can reason about jank, layout thrash, slow first paint, memory leaks and hydration cost from first principles instead of reciting tips.

## The multi-process architecture

Modern Chromium (Chrome, Edge, Brave, Opera, Arc) splits work across operating-system processes. Firefox (Fission) and Safari (WebKit) follow the same idea with different names.

| Process | Responsibility | Why it is separate |
|---|---|---|
| Browser process | UI chrome (tabs, address bar), navigation, network stack coordination, storage, permissions | Privileged: it is the only one that talks to the OS freely |
| Renderer process | Parses HTML/CSS, runs JavaScript (V8), builds DOM, style, layout, paint records | Sandboxed: it runs untrusted web content |
| GPU process | Talks to the GPU driver, rasterises and composites frames from all renderers | Driver crashes stay contained; one place owns the GPU |
| Network service | DNS, TCP/QUIC, TLS, HTTP cache | Can be restarted; isolates parsing of network bytes |
| Utility / storage / audio | Decoding, storage backends, audio | Least privilege |

**Site isolation.** Since 2018 desktop Chrome puts each *site* (scheme + registrable domain, e.g. `https://example.com`) in its own renderer process, including cross-site iframes ("out-of-process iframes"). The motivation was Spectre: if attacker JavaScript shares an address space with your bank's page, timing side channels can read memory. Process boundaries make that much harder. Consequences you should know:

- A cross-site iframe has its own main thread. A slow ad iframe does not block your main thread (but it still competes for CPU and the GPU).
- `postMessage` between cross-site frames is real inter-process communication.
- Headers such as `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy` and `Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy` make a page "cross-origin isolated", which unlocks `SharedArrayBuffer` and high-resolution timers.
- Memory use is higher; on low-memory Android devices Chrome applies isolation more selectively.

Inside one renderer process there are several threads that matter: the **main thread** (JS, style, layout, paint recording, most event handlers), the **compositor thread** (scrolling, layer transforms, frame production), **raster worker threads**, and any **Web Workers** you create.

## Navigation: from URL to first bytes

```text
User types URL
  -> Browser process: is it a search or a URL? check HSTS, service worker scope
  -> Network: DNS (often cached) -> TCP + TLS 1.3 (1 RTT) or QUIC/HTTP3 (often 1 RTT, 0-RTT on resume)
  -> HTTP request; response headers arrive
  -> Content-Type text/html + safe-browsing checks -> pick/commit a renderer process for the site
  -> Renderer streams the body into the HTML parser
```

Two things people miss: the browser can start a renderer **speculatively** while the request is in flight, and a **service worker** can answer the navigation without touching the network at all. Redirects each cost a full round trip, which is why `http -> https -> www` chains hurt Time to First Byte (TTFB).

## Parsing: HTML to DOM, CSS to CSSOM

The HTML parser is **incremental and streaming**: it builds DOM nodes as bytes arrive, which is why server streaming improves first paint. Rules that shape performance:

1. A classic script tag (no `async`, `defer` or `type="module"`) is **parser-blocking**: parsing stops, the script is fetched and executed, then parsing resumes. Scripts can call `document.write`, so the parser must wait.
2. CSS is **render-blocking**: the browser will not paint until the CSSOM for stylesheets in the head is ready, because painting unstyled content then restyling (a flash of unstyled content) is worse. CSS is also **script-blocking**: a script that follows a stylesheet waits for it, because the script may read computed styles.
3. The **preload scanner** is a second, lightweight parser that races ahead looking for `src` and `href` URLs to fetch early, even while the main parser is blocked. Content injected by JavaScript is invisible to it, which is why client-rendered hero images are discovered late.

| Script loading | Fetch | Execute | Order preserved |
|---|---|---|---|
| classic | blocks parser | immediately | yes |
| `async` | in parallel | as soon as downloaded (may interrupt parsing) | no |
| `defer` | in parallel | after parsing, before `DOMContentLoaded` | yes |
| `type="module"` | in parallel (deferred by default) | after parsing | yes |

## The rendering pipeline

Once DOM and CSSOM exist, every frame that needs visual updates goes through some or all of these stages:

```text
 JavaScript / events  (mutate DOM, classes, styles)
        |
   Style recalc       which CSS rules match which elements -> computed styles
        |
   Layout             geometry: x, y, width, height of every box (the layout tree)
        |
   Paint              record draw commands ("display list") per layer
        |
   Composite          raster tiles (GPU), position layers, draw the frame
```

- **Style.** Matching selectors against elements. Cost scales with the number of elements affected times selector complexity. Toggling a class on `body` can invalidate styles for the whole tree.
- **Layout (reflow).** Computes geometry. Nodes with `display: none` are not in the layout tree; pseudo-elements are. Layout is often the most expensive stage on big pages, and it can be scoped: `contain: layout` or `content-visibility: auto` limit how far a change propagates.
- **Paint.** Produces a list of drawing operations, not pixels. Large blur filters, shadows and gradients are expensive to raster later.
- **Composite.** The page is split into **layers**. Raster happens in tiles off the main thread (GPU raster in Chromium), and the compositor assembles layers into a frame. Animating `transform` and `opacity` on an element with its own layer can skip style, layout and paint entirely and run on the compositor thread, so it stays smooth even when the main thread is busy.

| You change | Stages that re-run |
|---|---|
| `width`, `top`, `font-size`, adding nodes | style, layout, paint, composite |
| `color`, `background-color`, `box-shadow` | style, paint, composite |
| `transform`, `opacity` (on its own layer) | composite only |

**Forced synchronous layout ("layout thrashing").** Layout is normally lazy: the browser batches DOM writes and lays out once before the next frame. But reading a geometry property (`offsetHeight`, `getBoundingClientRect()`, `scrollTop`, `getComputedStyle` for layout-dependent values) after a write forces layout *now*. Doing write, read, write, read in a loop forces layout on every iteration. The fix is to batch all reads, then all writes (or use `requestAnimationFrame` to write).

**Layers are not free.** `will-change: transform` promotes an element to its own layer. Each layer costs GPU memory (roughly width x height x 4 bytes per tile set), and too many layers make compositing slower. Promote only what actually animates, and remove the hint when the animation ends.

## Accessibility tree

The renderer also derives an **accessibility tree** from DOM + styles (roles, names, states). Screen readers consume it via OS accessibility APIs. It is a reason why semantic HTML matters for performance too: a `div` soup with ARIA patches makes this tree larger and harder to keep correct.

parts.label: Event loop, V8 and memory
parts.body:
## The event loop, precisely

The main thread runs one thing at a time. The HTML spec's event loop, simplified:

```text
loop forever:
  1. pick the oldest runnable task from a task queue
     (a timer, a network callback, an input event, a postMessage ...)
  2. run it to completion
  3. drain the microtask queue completely
     (promise reactions, queueMicrotask, MutationObserver callbacks)
  4. if it is time to render (roughly every display refresh) and something changed:
       a. run resize/scroll steps, media query changes
       b. run requestAnimationFrame callbacks
       c. style -> layout -> (ResizeObserver, IntersectionObserver checks) -> paint
       d. hand the frame to the compositor
  5. if idle time remains before the next frame, run requestIdleCallback callbacks
```

Key consequences:

- **Microtasks can starve rendering.** A promise chain that keeps queueing microtasks never yields; the page freezes just like with a `while (true)`.
- **`setTimeout(fn, 0)` is a task**, so it runs after microtasks and possibly after a render. Nested timers are clamped to at least 4 ms after five levels of nesting.
- **`requestAnimationFrame` runs right before style and layout** of the next frame, which makes it the right place for visual writes. It is paused in background tabs.
- Browsers prioritise task sources: input events are typically handled ahead of timers. The `scheduler.postTask()` API (Chromium) and `scheduler.yield()` let you express priorities explicitly; `scheduler.yield()` continues your work at the front of the queue after yielding, instead of the back.

## Frames and the 16.6 ms budget

On a 60 Hz display a new frame is due every 1000 / 60 = 16.67 ms. On 120 Hz screens it is 8.33 ms. Your JavaScript is not the only thing in that budget: style, layout, paint and compositing need time too, so a practical target is **under ~10 ms of script per frame** during animations and scrolling.

```text
|<------------------- 16.6 ms frame ------------------->|
| input | JS (rAF, handlers) | style | layout | paint | composite |  idle  |
                                                         ^ vsync: frame shown
```

A **long task** is any task over **50 ms**. The 50 ms figure comes from the RAIL model: to respond to input within 100 ms, work must be split into chunks small enough that an input arriving mid-chunk still gets handled quickly. Long tasks are what hurts **Interaction to Next Paint (INP)**.

If a frame misses its deadline the compositor shows the previous frame again (a dropped frame). Scrolling usually stays smooth anyway because the compositor thread can scroll already-rastered layers without the main thread, unless there is a non-passive `touchstart`/`wheel` listener, which forces the compositor to wait for JavaScript. That is why `{ passive: true }` matters.

## The JavaScript engine pipeline (V8)

V8 (Chrome, Node.js, Deno) compiles in tiers. The names change over time, but the shape is stable:

```text
source -> parser -> AST -> Ignition (bytecode interpreter)
                               |  collects type feedback per call site
                               v
                         Sparkplug (fast baseline compiler, no optimisation)
                               v
                         Maglev (mid-tier optimising compiler)
                               v
                         TurboFan (top-tier optimising compiler)
                               |
               speculation fails (types change) -> deoptimise back to bytecode
```

- **Lazy parsing.** V8 pre-parses functions quickly and fully parses only when they are called. Shipping less JavaScript still matters because download, decompression, parse and compile are all on the critical path, and compile work is partially on the main thread.
- **Hidden classes (shapes) and inline caches.** Objects created with the same properties in the same order share a hidden class; a property access site that always sees one shape is "monomorphic" and becomes a fixed-offset load. Sites that see many shapes become "megamorphic" and slower. Practical rule: initialise all fields in constructors, in the same order, and do not `delete` properties on hot objects.
- **Deoptimisation.** TurboFan speculates on types from feedback. Passing a string where it has only seen numbers throws away optimised code. This rarely matters for app code but explains odd benchmarks.
- **Code caching.** V8 caches compiled bytecode for scripts loaded repeatedly, which makes repeat visits cheaper. Changing a bundle's content hash on every deploy invalidates this cache; stable chunking helps.

## Memory and garbage collection

V8 uses a **generational** collector, Orinoco:

| Space | What lives there | Collection |
|---|---|---|
| Young generation (nursery) | New, short-lived objects | Scavenger: frequent, fast, parallel copying |
| Old generation | Objects that survived two scavenges | Mark-compact: concurrent marking, incremental, parallel compaction |
| Large object space | Big allocations | Not moved |

Most objects die young, so scavenges are cheap. Old-generation marking runs mostly concurrently on helper threads, but some pauses remain on the main thread. Allocation-heavy code in animation loops (creating arrays or closures per frame) causes frequent collections and frame drops.

**Common frontend leaks** (memory that is still reachable, so GC cannot free it):

1. Event listeners on `window` or `document` added in a component and never removed.
2. Detached DOM nodes still referenced from a JavaScript array, cache or closure.
3. Unbounded caches and `Map`s keyed by objects (use `WeakMap` when keys should not keep values alive).
4. Timers and intervals never cleared; subscriptions (WebSocket, store) never unsubscribed.
5. Closures capturing a large scope, such as a handler that closes over a whole data array.

Find them with the DevTools **Memory** panel: take a heap snapshot, perform the action several times, take another snapshot, compare, and search for "Detached" elements. The retainers view shows the path keeping an object alive.

## Putting it together: one click, end to end

```text
1. OS delivers the click to the browser process
2. Browser process routes it to the renderer that owns that pixel (hit-testing on the compositor)
3. Compositor queues an input task on the renderer main thread
4. Main thread runs your click handler (task) -> setState -> microtasks drain
5. Framework re-renders, mutates DOM
6. Next rendering opportunity: rAF -> style -> layout -> paint -> commit to compositor
7. GPU process composites and the display shows the frame
   INP for this interaction = time from step 1 to step 7
```

Every optimisation you will learn maps to shrinking one of those steps: less work in step 4 (yield, debounce, move to a worker), less DOM churn in step 5 (memoisation, virtualisation), cheaper step 6 (avoid layout-affecting animations, contain layout), and fewer layers or cheaper paint effects in step 7.

parts.label: Interview
parts.body:
## What interviewers are really testing

Browser-internals questions are a proxy for "can this person debug performance problems they have never seen before?". Senior candidates are expected to connect a symptom (janky scroll, slow first paint, a page that grows to 2 GB) to a stage of the pipeline and a tool to prove it. Reciting "the DOM is a tree" is not enough; naming the cost of each stage and how to measure it is.

## Question 1: "What happens when you type a URL and press Enter?"

**Model answer (aim for 2 minutes, then let them steer):**

> The browser process decides it is a URL, checks HSTS and whether a service worker controls the scope. The network service resolves DNS, opens a connection (TCP plus TLS 1.3, or QUIC for HTTP/3) and sends the request. When response headers arrive and the content type is HTML, the browser commits the navigation to a renderer process chosen by site isolation. The renderer streams bytes into the HTML parser, which builds the DOM incrementally while the preload scanner fetches subresources early. Stylesheets block rendering, classic scripts block parsing. Once the DOM and CSSOM are ready enough, the main thread computes style, layout and paint records, and the compositor rasterises tiles on the GPU and shows the first frame. From there the event loop handles input, timers and rendering opportunities.

Depth signals they look for: preload scanner, render-blocking vs parser-blocking, streaming parse, compositor thread, site isolation. Offer to go deeper into any stage: "I can go into TLS, caching or the rendering pipeline, whichever is most useful."

## Question 2: "Why is animating `transform` cheaper than animating `left`?"

**Model answer:** Changing `left` changes geometry, so every frame re-runs style, layout, paint and composite on the main thread, and layout can cascade to siblings and ancestors. `transform` on an element with its own compositor layer only changes how an already-rastered layer is positioned, so the compositor thread can do it without the main thread at all. That also means the animation stays smooth when JavaScript is busy. The trade-off is layer memory: promote only elements that actually animate.

## Question 3: "Explain the event loop. What does this print?"

```ts
console.log('A');
setTimeout(() => console.log('B'), 0);
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('C'));
queueMicrotask(() => console.log('D'));
requestAnimationFrame(() => console.log('E'));
console.log('F');
```

**Model answer:** `A F C D` first: synchronous code, then the microtask queue drains in order (`C`, then `D`). After that, `B` and `E` race: the timer is a task, `rAF` runs at the next rendering opportunity. In practice `B` usually prints before `E`, but the order is not guaranteed by the spec, and in a background tab `E` may not fire at all. Saying "it depends, and here is why" scores higher than a confident wrong order.

## Question 4: "What is layout thrashing and how do you fix it?"

**Model answer:** Reading a layout-dependent property after writing to the DOM forces the browser to run layout synchronously so the value is correct. Interleaving writes and reads in a loop forces a layout per iteration, turning one layout into N. Fix it by batching reads before writes, caching measurements, scheduling writes in `requestAnimationFrame`, or using `ResizeObserver` instead of polling sizes. In DevTools it shows as purple "Layout" blocks with a "Forced reflow" warning attached to your function.

## Question 5: "Our page leaks memory in a long session. How do you find it?"

**Model answer:** Reproduce with a repeatable action (open and close a modal 10 times). In the Memory panel, take a heap snapshot before and after, use the comparison view and sort by delta. Look for "Detached" DOM trees and growing arrays or maps, then follow the retainers path to the code holding the reference: typically a global listener, a store subscription or a cache. Fix with cleanup in effect teardowns, `AbortController` for listeners and fetches, `WeakMap` for object-keyed caches, and bounded LRU caches. Verify the fix by repeating the snapshot comparison.

## Question 6: "Why did browsers move to site isolation?"

**Model answer:** Spectre-class attacks showed that code in one address space can read other memory in the same process via timing side channels. Putting each site in its own sandboxed process means attacker JavaScript cannot share memory with your bank's page. It costs memory and makes cross-site frames use inter-process communication, and it is why cross-origin isolation headers (COOP and COEP) gate powerful features like `SharedArrayBuffer`.

## Follow-ups that separate seniors

| Follow-up | What a strong answer includes |
|---|---|
| "How would you keep a 60 fps animation while a heavy computation runs?" | Animate on the compositor (`transform`/`opacity`), move computation to a Web Worker, or chunk it with `scheduler.yield()` |
| "Why might a page be blank for 3 s on a fast network?" | Render-blocking CSS or fonts, a large client-rendered bundle, a slow server (TTFB), or blocking third-party scripts in the head |
| "What is the compositor thread allowed to do without the main thread?" | Scroll, pinch-zoom, and run transform/opacity animations on promoted layers, unless blocked by non-passive listeners |
| "How does V8 make property access fast?" | Hidden classes plus inline caches; keep object shapes stable |

## Common mistakes

- Saying "the virtual DOM makes it fast". The browser pipeline still runs; a virtual DOM only reduces how much DOM you touch.
- Claiming `async` scripts never block. They do not block the parser while downloading, but they execute on the main thread whenever they arrive, possibly mid-parse.
- Forgetting that CSS blocks rendering, and that fonts can hide text (FOIT) unless `font-display` is set.
- Treating `will-change` as a free speed-up.
- Confusing microtasks with tasks, or claiming `setTimeout(0)` runs "immediately".

keyPoints: Chromium splits work into browser, renderer, GPU and network processes; site isolation gives each site its own sandboxed renderer as a Spectre defence.
CSS is render-blocking; classic scripts are parser-blocking; the preload scanner fetches resources it can see in the HTML early.
The pipeline is style, layout, paint, composite; transform and opacity on a promoted layer skip the first three and run on the compositor thread.
Reading geometry after writing to the DOM forces synchronous layout; batch reads before writes.
One task, then all microtasks, then maybe a render: microtasks can starve frames, and tasks over 50 ms are long tasks that hurt INP.
V8 tiers from Ignition bytecode through Sparkplug and Maglev to TurboFan, guided by type feedback; stable object shapes keep code fast.
Generational GC makes short-lived objects cheap; leaks are references you forgot, found by comparing heap snapshots.

check.q: Which change can be applied by the compositor thread without re-running style, layout or paint, assuming the element already has its own layer?
options: Changing width from 200px to 300px
Changing background-color
Changing transform: translateX(...)
Appending a child node
check.why: Transform (and opacity) on a promoted layer only changes how existing raster tiles are composited, so the compositor can do it off the main thread. Width and new nodes need layout; colour needs paint.

check.q: A loop sets el.style.height and then reads el.offsetHeight for 500 elements. What is the main cost?
options: 500 garbage collections
Up to 500 forced synchronous layouts
500 network requests
500 compositor layers
check.why: Each read after a write forces layout so the value is accurate. Batching all reads before all writes reduces it to one layout.

check.q: In what order do these run: synchronous code, a resolved promise's then callback, and a setTimeout(fn, 0)?
options: Synchronous, then the promise callback, then the timeout
Synchronous, then the timeout, then the promise callback
Promise callback, synchronous, timeout
The order is random
check.why: The current task finishes, then the microtask queue (promise reactions) drains completely, and only then can the event loop pick the next task such as a timer.

lessons.title: Rendering strategies: CSR to Server Components
lessons.summary: CSR, SSR, SSG, ISR, streaming, React Server Components, islands and edge rendering: what each sends on the wire, what hydration costs, how to choose per route, and the caching layers behind them.

parts.label: Concepts
parts.body:
## The one question behind every strategy

Every rendering strategy answers the same question differently: **where and when is the HTML for this request produced, and how much JavaScript must run in the browser before the page is interactive?** Keep three timelines in mind for each one: when the server responds (TTFB), when meaningful pixels appear (FCP and LCP), and when the page responds to input (hydration done, INP).

## Client-side rendering (CSR)

The server (usually a CDN) returns an almost empty HTML shell plus a JavaScript bundle. The browser downloads, parses and runs the bundle, which fetches data and renders the UI.

```text
Browser                      CDN                API
  | GET /dashboard ---------> |                  |
  | <--- shell.html (2 KB) -- |                  |
  | GET app.[hash].js ------> |                  |
  | <--- 300 KB gzip -------- |                  |
  | parse + execute JS ...    |                  |
  | GET /api/me, /api/items ---------------------> |
  | <-------------------------------- JSON ------ |
  | render -> first meaningful paint (late)      |
```

- **Strengths:** trivially cacheable static hosting, rich app-like interactions, no server to scale, simple mental model.
- **Weaknesses:** LCP waits on JS download plus execution plus a data round trip (a waterfall); poor on slow phones; crawlers that do not run JavaScript see nothing; large bundles hurt INP.
- **Fits:** authenticated tools where SEO is irrelevant and sessions are long: Gmail, Figma's editor, admin consoles, internal dashboards.

## Server-side rendering (SSR)

The server renders HTML per request with data already in it. The browser paints quickly, then downloads the same components' JavaScript and **hydrates**: React walks the existing DOM, attaches event handlers and rebuilds its internal tree.

```text
Browser                      Server               DB/API
  | GET /product/42 -------> | fetch data -------> |
  |                          | <------------------ |
  |                          | renderToString/stream
  | <--- full HTML ---------- |                    |
  | paint (FCP/LCP early)     |                    |
  | GET bundle.js, hydrate -> interactive (later)  |
```

- **Strengths:** fast first paint with real content, SEO-friendly, per-request personalisation.
- **Weaknesses:** TTFB includes data fetching; servers must scale with traffic; you pay twice (render on server, hydrate on client); the "uncanny valley" where the page looks ready but clicks do nothing until hydration finishes.

## Static site generation (SSG)

HTML is rendered **at build time** and served from a CDN. Identical to SSR from the browser's point of view, but TTFB is CDN-fast because nothing runs per request.

- **Fits:** docs, marketing pages, blogs. Most documentation sites built with Next.js, Astro, Docusaurus or VitePress are static.
- **Limits:** build time grows with page count; content is stale until the next build; no per-user content in the HTML.

## Incremental static regeneration (ISR)

ISR is SSG with a cache lifetime. Pages are generated on first request (or at build time) and cached; after the revalidation window, the next request gets the **stale page immediately** while a regeneration runs in the background (stale-while-revalidate). On-demand revalidation lets a CMS webhook or a Server Action invalidate by path or tag.

In the Next.js App Router you get this through route segment config (`export const revalidate = 300`), `fetch(url, { next: { revalidate: 300, tags: ['product-42'] } })`, or, with Cache Components enabled, the `'use cache'` directive with `cacheLife` and `cacheTag`. Invalidation uses `revalidatePath`, `revalidateTag(tag, 'max')` for stale-while-revalidate semantics, or `updateTag` inside a Server Action when the user must see their own write immediately.

- **Fits:** e-commerce catalogues, news articles, listing pages: millions of pages, mostly read, tolerate seconds to minutes of staleness.

## Streaming SSR

Instead of waiting for all data before sending anything, the server **flushes the HTML shell immediately** and streams the rest as each data dependency resolves. In React 18+ this is `renderToPipeableStream` / `renderToReadableStream` plus `Suspense` boundaries; in Next.js, `loading.tsx` and `Suspense` do it for you.

```text
t=0ms    <html><head>...css...</head><body><nav/><main><!--fallback skeleton-->
t=40ms   (headers sent, browser starts fetching CSS/JS, paints the shell)
t=300ms  <template> for reviews + inline script that swaps it into place
t=900ms  recommendations chunk arrives and swaps in
```

Each `Suspense` boundary can also **hydrate independently** (selective hydration), and React prioritises hydrating the boundary the user is interacting with. The slow recommendation service no longer delays TTFB or the hero.

**Gotchas:** once headers are sent you cannot change the status code or redirect with a 3xx (frameworks fall back to a client-side redirect or meta tag); proxies that buffer responses break streaming; put SEO-critical content outside slow boundaries.

## React Server Components (RSC)

Server Components run **only on the server** (at build or request time). Their code never ships to the browser. They can be `async`, read databases directly and pass serialisable props to **Client Components** (marked `"use client"`), which are the only parts that hydrate.

On the wire, the server produces the **RSC payload**: a compact streamed description of the rendered tree, with references to client component modules and their props. On first load it is embedded alongside the HTML; on client navigation the router fetches just the payload and React reconciles it into the existing tree without a full reload, preserving client state.

```text
Server Component tree           RSC payload (conceptually)
  Page (server)                   ["$","main",null,{children:[
    ProductInfo (server)             ["$","h1",null,{children:"Trail shoe"}],
    AddToCart (client) -------->     ["$","$L1",null,{sku:"42"}]   // $L1 = ref to client chunk
    Reviews (server, async)          "$@2" ]}]                      // streamed later
```

- **Win:** less JavaScript (markdown parsers, date libraries and data-fetching code stay on the server), no client-server waterfalls for data, secrets stay server-side.
- **Cost:** a new mental model (the server/client boundary, serialisable props only, no hooks in server components), framework coupling, and caching becomes a central concern.

## Islands architecture

Render the page as static HTML and hydrate only **isolated interactive widgets** ("islands"), each with its own small bundle. Astro popularised it (`client:load`, `client:visible`, `client:idle` directives); Fresh (Deno) uses it too. RSC achieves a similar outcome inside React, but islands are framework-agnostic and do not need a shared root.

- **Fits:** content-heavy sites with a few widgets (a search box, a carousel, a cart button).
- **Weakness:** sharing state across islands needs extra plumbing (a small store, custom events); full-page app-like navigation is not the default.

## Edge rendering

Run SSR or middleware in data centres close to the user (Vercel, Cloudflare Workers, Netlify Edge). The runtime is usually a V8 isolate with web-standard APIs (`fetch`, `Request`, `Response`) and limits on CPU time, package size and Node.js APIs.

The trap: **rendering at the edge only helps if the data is also near the edge.** If the edge function in Mumbai calls a database in Virginia three times, you have added three cross-ocean round trips. Edge works well for personalisation from cookies, A/B assignment, geolocation redirects, auth checks, and pages backed by a globally replicated or cached data store.

## Partial prerendering (a hybrid worth knowing)

Next.js can combine a static shell with dynamic holes in one route: the static parts are served instantly from the CDN and the dynamic parts stream in from the server in the same response. In Next.js 16 this is part of Cache Components. It answers the classic dilemma "the page is 90% static but shows the user's cart count".

parts.label: Hydration, choice, caching
parts.body:
## Hydration in detail

Hydration is the step that makes server HTML interactive. React must:

1. Download and execute the JavaScript for every component in the hydrated tree.
2. Re-run those components (render, not commit) to rebuild the virtual tree.
3. Walk the existing DOM, match it to that tree, and attach event listeners (React uses event delegation at the root).

**Hydration mismatches** happen when server and client render different output: `Date.now()`, `Math.random()`, `typeof window` branches, locale formatting, or browser extensions injecting nodes. React 18+ recovers by client-rendering the nearest Suspense boundary, which costs performance and logs an error. Fixes: render time-dependent content in an effect, pass the server value down, or use `suppressHydrationWarning` for a single text node such as a timestamp.

**Why hydration is expensive:** it is proportional to the size of the hydrated tree, not to how interactive it is. A 2,000-node article with one "like" button hydrates 2,000 nodes. Every strategy after SSR is essentially about hydrating less:

| Technique | How it reduces hydration |
|---|---|
| Selective hydration (React 18) | Hydrates Suspense boundaries independently, prioritising what the user touches |
| Server Components | Server-only components never hydrate; only Client Component subtrees do |
| Islands | Only marked widgets hydrate; the rest is inert HTML |
| Resumability (Qwik) | Serialises framework state into HTML; resumes on interaction instead of replaying renders |
| Lazy hydration | Hydrate a widget when visible or idle |

## The decision matrix

| Strategy | TTFB | LCP | JS shipped | Freshness | Personalised | Server cost | SEO |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| CSR | Fastest (static) | Slow (JS + data waterfall) | Most | Real time | Yes (client) | None | Weak |
| SSR | Slower (data on path) | Fast | All components | Real time | Yes | Per request | Strong |
| Streaming SSR | Fast (shell) | Fast | All components | Real time | Yes | Per request | Strong if content outside slow boundaries |
| SSG | Fastest (CDN) | Fast | All components | Build time | No | None | Strong |
| ISR | CDN fast (stale ok) | Fast | All components | Seconds to minutes | No (or via client) | On revalidation | Strong |
| RSC + streaming | Fast | Fast | Client components only | Configurable per component | Yes | Per request (cacheable parts) | Strong |
| Islands | CDN fast | Fast | Islands only | Build or request | Limited | Low | Strong |
| Edge SSR | Fast if data is near | Fast | Same as SSR | Real time | Yes | Per request, cheap per call | Strong |

**A practical way to choose, per route, not per app:**

```text
Is the content the same for every user?
 |- yes: Does it change more often than you deploy?
 |       |- no  -> SSG
 |       |- yes -> ISR / cached server components with tag invalidation
 |- no (personalised):
         Does it need SEO or a fast first paint on mobile?
         |- yes -> streaming SSR with RSC; static shell + dynamic holes (PPR)
         |- no  -> CSR behind auth is fine (still code-split it)
Is it mostly content with a few widgets? -> islands or RSC with tiny client components
```

Real apps mix strategies: the marketing site is static, product pages are ISR, the cart is streamed SSR with a client component, and the account dashboard is effectively CSR behind auth.

## Caching layers

Rendering strategy and caching are the same conversation. A request may be answered at any of these layers:

```text
Browser memory cache / bfcache
  -> Service worker cache (if any)
    -> Browser HTTP cache (Cache-Control, ETag)
      -> CDN edge cache (s-maxage, stale-while-revalidate, surrogate keys/tags)
        -> Framework cache (Next.js data cache, 'use cache', full-route cache)
          -> Application cache (Redis, in-memory LRU)
            -> Database
```

| Header | Meaning | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable` | Cache for a year, never revalidate | Hashed assets (`app.3f9a1c.js`) |
| `Cache-Control: public, s-maxage=60, stale-while-revalidate=600` | CDN fresh for 60 s, may serve stale for 10 min while refetching | ISR-like HTML at the CDN |
| `Cache-Control: private, no-cache` | Browser may store but must revalidate (ETag) every time | Personalised HTML |
| `Cache-Control: no-store` | Never store | Banking pages, sensitive responses |
| `Vary: Accept-Encoding, Cookie` | Cache key includes these headers | Avoid serving one user's page to another |

Rules worth stating in an interview:

- **Hash static assets and cache them forever; never cache HTML forever.** The HTML is the pointer to the current asset hashes.
- **Never let a CDN cache a personalised response** without the personalisation in the cache key. Leaking one user's account page to others is a classic incident.
- **The back/forward cache (bfcache)** restores a whole page from memory on back navigation. `unload` listeners and `Cache-Control: no-store` on the HTML can make a page ineligible in some browsers.
- **Invalidation by tag beats invalidation by time** for content that changes on events (a price update). CDNs call them surrogate keys or cache tags.

## Who uses what (well-documented patterns)

| Product type | Typical strategy | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Docs and blogs (React docs, Next.js docs, most OSS docs) | SSG | Content changes on deploy; CDN-fast everywhere |
| Large e-commerce catalogues | ISR or cached SSR + client islands for cart and price | Millions of pages, SEO critical, staleness of seconds is fine |
| Social feeds | Streaming SSR shell + client data fetching for the infinite feed | First paint fast, then app-like behaviour |
| Editors and design tools (Figma, Google Docs) | CSR (canvas or heavy client state) | Session length makes initial cost acceptable; interactivity is everything |
| Webmail and admin consoles (Gmail) | CSR / SPA | Behind login, no SEO, long sessions |
| Content sites with widgets | Islands (Astro) | Ship almost no JS |

Note the pattern: the longer the session and the less SEO matters, the more CSR is acceptable. The shorter the session (someone landing from search), the more first-load cost dominates and the more you push to the server.

## Measuring the trade-off, not guessing

Before switching strategies, measure the actual bottleneck:

- High **TTFB** with SSR: the data fetch is slow. Cache it, stream around it, or parallelise fetches (avoid sequential `await`s).
- High **LCP** with CSR: the LCP element is discovered late. SSR or prerender the hero, or at least preload its image.
- Poor **INP** after SSR: hydration and large bundles are blocking the main thread. Reduce client components, split code, defer third parties.
- High **CLS** with streaming: fallbacks that are a different size than the content. Make skeletons the same dimensions.

diagrams.title: Choosing a strategy per route

parts.label: Interview
parts.body:
## What interviewers are really testing

Rendering questions check whether you pick strategies **per route from requirements**, understand the costs on the wire (TTFB, bytes, hydration), and know that caching is part of the answer. The weakest answers name a framework ("we use Next.js so it is SSR"). The strongest answers walk through a timeline and a cache.

## Question 1: "SSR vs CSR: when would you choose each?"

**Model answer:**

> It depends on who lands on the page and how long they stay. CSR ships a shell and does everything in the browser, so first paint waits on the bundle and a data round trip, but hosting is static and long sessions feel app-like. That is fine for an authenticated dashboard. SSR renders HTML with data per request, so first paint and SEO are good, but TTFB includes the data fetch, I pay server cost per request, and the client still downloads and hydrates the same components. For a landing or product page reached from search on a mid-range phone, SSR or static generation wins clearly. In practice I choose per route, and with React Server Components I can keep most of the tree on the server and hydrate only the interactive parts.

## Question 2: "Explain hydration and why it can hurt INP."

**Model answer:** Hydration re-runs the component tree on the client against server-rendered DOM and attaches handlers. Its cost scales with the size of the hydrated tree, and it runs as JavaScript on the main thread, often as long tasks right when the user starts interacting. Clicks during that window either do nothing or queue behind hydration, which shows up as poor INP. Mitigations: fewer and smaller client components (RSC), Suspense boundaries for selective hydration, code splitting, and deferring non-critical widgets until visible or idle.

## Question 3: "Design the rendering for an e-commerce product page with 5 million SKUs."

**Model answer (structure it):**

1. **Requirements:** SEO critical, mobile-heavy traffic, price and stock change often, the cart is personal, reviews are slow to load.
2. **Strategy:** product description and images as cached server components or ISR, tagged `product-{id}`; the CMS or pricing service calls tag invalidation on change. Price and stock either in the cached part with short revalidation or in a small streamed section. Cart button and size picker are tiny client components. Reviews and recommendations stream behind Suspense with same-size skeletons.
3. **Caching:** hashed assets immutable at the CDN; HTML with `s-maxage` plus `stale-while-revalidate`; personalised bits never in the shared cached HTML.
4. **Generation:** do not prebuild 5 million pages; prebuild the top few thousand by traffic and generate the rest on first request.
5. **Measure:** LCP is the hero image, so it is in the HTML with `fetchpriority="high"` and correct dimensions; track field LCP and INP by template.

## Question 4: "What do React Server Components actually send over the network?"

**Model answer:** On first load you get HTML for a fast paint plus the RSC payload inline, which describes the rendered server tree, with placeholders that reference Client Component chunks and their serialised props. On client-side navigation the router fetches only the RSC payload for the new route segment and React merges it into the current tree, so client state in shared layouts survives. Server Component code, and libraries used only there, are never downloaded. Props crossing to the client must be serialisable, so no functions except Server Actions.

## Question 5: "When does edge rendering make things slower?"

**Model answer:** When the data is not at the edge. Each sequential query from an edge location to a single-region database pays a long round trip, so a page with three dependent queries can be slower than rendering in the database's region. Edge is good for logic that needs only the request (cookies, geo, headers) or globally replicated data. Otherwise run the render near the data and cache at the edge.

## Question 6: "How would you avoid serving one user's page to another from the CDN?"

**Model answer:** Mark personalised HTML `Cache-Control: private` or `no-store`, keep shared pages free of personal data and fetch personal bits client-side or in a separately cached request, and if the CDN must vary, include the dimension in the cache key explicitly (a segment cookie, not the whole cookie header). Audit with a test that requests the same URL with two sessions and compares responses.

## Quick-fire follow-ups

| Follow-up | Strong short answer |
|---|---|
| "ISR vs SSR with a CDN cache?" | Similar effect; ISR makes the framework own regeneration and invalidation, SSR + `s-maxage` relies on CDN headers |
| "Can you redirect after streaming starts?" | Not with an HTTP status; headers are sent. Frameworks inject a client redirect instead |
| "What breaks streaming?" | Buffering proxies or compression middleware, `await`ing everything at the top of the page, no Suspense boundaries |
| "Islands vs RSC?" | Both hydrate only interactive parts. Islands are framework-agnostic and per-widget; RSC is one React tree with client navigation and shared state |
| "Hydration mismatch causes?" | Time, randomness, locale, `window` checks, invalid HTML nesting (a `div` inside a `p`), extensions |

## Common mistakes

- Treating the whole app as one strategy instead of choosing per route.
- Saying SSR "is faster" without separating TTFB, LCP and interactivity.
- Forgetting that SSR still ships and runs all component JavaScript for hydration.
- Putting `"use client"` at the top of a layout, which turns its whole subtree into client code.
- Ignoring caching headers, or caching personalised HTML at the CDN.
- Choosing edge rendering without asking where the data lives.

keyPoints: Every strategy answers where and when HTML is produced and how much JavaScript must run before the page is interactive.
SSR improves first paint and SEO but still ships and hydrates every component; hydration cost scales with tree size, not interactivity.
Streaming SSR flushes a shell immediately and streams Suspense boundaries as data resolves; selective hydration prioritises what the user touches.
Server Components never ship their code; only Client Component subtrees hydrate, and navigation fetches the RSC payload, not HTML.
Choose per route: static for shared content, ISR or tagged caches for content that changes, streaming RSC for personalised SEO pages, CSR behind auth.
Hash assets and cache them forever; never cache HTML forever; never let a CDN cache personalised responses.
Edge rendering helps only when the data is near the edge too.

check.q: A blog with 2,000 articles updates a few articles per day from a CMS. Which approach best balances speed and freshness?
options: Client-side rendering with an API call per article
Static/ISR pages with on-demand tag invalidation from a CMS webhook
Full SSR on every request with no caching
Edge SSR querying a single-region database
check.why: Content is the same for everyone and changes on events, so CDN-served static pages invalidated by tag on publish give CDN-fast TTFB and near-immediate freshness.

check.q: Why can a server-rendered page look ready but ignore clicks for a second on a mid-range phone?
options: The CDN has not finished caching it
CSS is still render-blocking
Hydration is still downloading and running component JavaScript on the main thread
The browser is garbage collecting the DOM
check.why: SSR HTML paints early, but handlers attach only after hydration re-runs the components on the main thread; large trees and bundles extend that window and hurt INP.

check.q: What does the browser download when navigating client-side between two App Router pages built mostly from Server Components?
options: The RSC payload for the new segment plus any new Client Component chunks
A full HTML document and the entire bundle again
The Server Components' source code
Nothing; everything was prefetched at build time
check.why: The router requests the serialised RSC payload and merges it into the current tree; server component code never ships, and only client chunks not yet loaded are fetched.

lessons.title: Performance engineering and Core Web Vitals
lessons.summary: LCP, INP and CLS and how they are measured, lab vs field, reading a DevTools trace, main-thread work, code splitting, images, fonts, third parties, budgets in CI, and a slow-to-good case study.

parts.label: Metrics and measurement
parts.body:
## Core Web Vitals: what is actually measured

Google's Core Web Vitals are three user-centric metrics. Each is judged at the **75th percentile** of real page loads, separately for mobile and desktop. A page "passes" when all three are good at p75.

| Metric | Measures | Good | Needs improvement | Poor |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **LCP** Largest Contentful Paint | Loading: when the largest image or text block in the viewport rendered | <= 2.5 s | 2.5 to 4 s | > 4 s |
| **INP** Interaction to Next Paint | Responsiveness: latency from input to the next frame, across the visit | <= 200 ms | 200 to 500 ms | > 500 ms |
| **CLS** Cumulative Layout Shift | Visual stability: unexpected movement of content | <= 0.1 | 0.1 to 0.25 | > 0.25 |

INP replaced First Input Delay (FID) as a Core Web Vital in March 2024. FID only measured the *delay before the first* interaction's handler started; INP measures the full latency of (nearly) *all* interactions and reports roughly the worst one (for pages with many interactions, a high percentile, ignoring one outlier per 50 interactions).

### LCP, broken into sub-parts

LCP is not one number to optimise; it is four phases, and the fix depends on which one dominates:

```text
navigation start
 |-- TTFB ----------|-- resource load delay --|-- resource load duration --|-- element render delay --| LCP
   server + network   time until the browser     downloading the image       time from loaded to
   + redirects        even starts fetching the   (or font for text LCP)      painted (blocked by JS,
                      LCP resource                                           CSS, hydration)
```

Rough guidance from web.dev: TTFB and load duration together should be most of the time; **load delay and render delay should be close to zero**. In practice the biggest wins are usually load delay (the image was discovered late because it was injected by JavaScript or lazy-loaded) and render delay (render-blocking CSS or client rendering).

Candidate elements: `img`, `image` inside SVG, `video` poster or first frame, elements with a CSS `background-image` loaded via `url()`, and block-level text. The LCP element can change during load as larger content appears; the browser stops reporting new candidates after the first user input.

### INP, broken into sub-parts

```text
user taps
 |-- input delay --|-- processing duration --|-- presentation delay --| next frame painted
   main thread busy    your event handlers       style, layout, paint of
   with other tasks    (all listeners)           the update + compositing
```

- **Input delay** is high when a long task (hydration, analytics, a big JSON parse) is running when the user taps.
- **Processing duration** is high when handlers do too much synchronously (big state updates, re-rendering huge lists).
- **Presentation delay** is high when the resulting DOM change is large or triggers expensive layout.

### CLS, how it is scored

Each unexpected layout shift has a score = **impact fraction x distance fraction** (how much of the viewport moved, times how far, relative to the viewport). Shifts are grouped into **session windows** (shifts less than 1 s apart, window capped at 5 s), and CLS is the **largest window's** total. Shifts within 500 ms of a user input (a click that expands an accordion) are excluded, because they are expected. Animations using `transform` do not count as layout shifts.

Usual causes: images and embeds without dimensions, ads and banners injected above content, web fonts swapping with different metrics, and client-side content inserted above what the user is reading.

## Lab vs field data

| | Lab (synthetic) | Field (RUM) |
|---|---|---|
| Tools | Lighthouse, DevTools Performance panel, WebPageTest | Chrome UX Report (CrUX), PageSpeed Insights field section, Search Console, your own RUM via `web-vitals` |
| Conditions | One controlled device and network profile | Real users, devices, networks, caches |
| INP | Not measurable without interaction; Lighthouse uses **Total Blocking Time (TBT)** as a proxy | Measured directly |
| Good for | Debugging, regression testing in CI, reproducibility | The truth: what users experience and what Google uses |
| Weakness | May not match your users at all | Noisy, delayed (CrUX is a 28-day rolling window), less diagnostic detail |

The workflow: **field data tells you which page and metric is bad; lab tools tell you why.** A common surprise is good Lighthouse scores and bad field INP, because Lighthouse loads the page without interacting and on a cold cache, while real users tap during hydration on low-end Android phones.

To make field data diagnostic, send attribution with your RUM beacons: the `web-vitals` library's attribution build reports the LCP element and its sub-part timings, the INP target element, interaction type and phase breakdown, and the largest shift source for CLS.

## Profiling with the DevTools Performance panel

How to read a trace, step by step:

1. Open DevTools in an incognito window (extensions add noise), Performance panel, enable **CPU throttling (4x or 6x)** and a network preset to approximate a mid-range phone.
2. Record a page load (the reload button) or record while performing the slow interaction.
3. Read the top **tracks**: Frames (green and red bars show dropped frames), Interactions (each interaction with its INP-style duration), Network waterfall, and **Main** thread.
4. In Main, long tasks have a red triangle and a striped section past 50 ms. Click one; the **Bottom-Up** tab shows which functions consumed self time, **Call Tree** shows the hierarchy, and the summary shows scripting vs rendering vs painting.
5. Look for purple blocks (style and layout). A "Forced reflow" warning points to layout thrashing in your code.
6. The Timings track marks LCP, FCP and DCL; the **Layout shifts** track shows which nodes moved.
7. The live metrics view in recent Chrome versions shows local LCP, INP and CLS as you use the page, alongside CrUX field data for comparison.

The **Long Animation Frames (LoAF) API** (Chromium) is the field counterpart: it reports frames that took over 50 ms with script attribution (which script URL and function), which is far more useful than the older Long Tasks API for finding the culprit in production.

## Main-thread work: the root of bad INP

The main thread is shared by your app, the framework, every third-party script and the browser's rendering work. Strategies, in order of usual impact:

1. **Do less.** Remove unused code and dependencies; avoid re-rendering what did not change (memoisation, stable props, splitting contexts); virtualise long lists.
2. **Do it later.** Defer non-critical work until after the next paint: show the visual response first, then run analytics or persistence. Patterns: `requestAnimationFrame` followed by `setTimeout`, `scheduler.postTask` with background priority, `requestIdleCallback`.
3. **Break it up.** Yield inside long loops (`scheduler.yield()`), so input can be processed between chunks.
4. **Do it elsewhere.** Move pure computation (parsing, diffing, search indexing, image processing) to a Web Worker; Comlink makes the messaging pleasant.
5. **Let React help.** `startTransition` and `useDeferredValue` mark updates as interruptible, so typing stays responsive while a heavy result list re-renders.

diagrams.code:
sequenceDiagram
  participant U as User
  participant M as Main thread
  participant C as Compositor / GPU
  U->>M: tap (queued behind a long task)
  Note over M: input delay (hydration, third-party script)
  M->>M: event handlers run (processing duration)
  M->>M: style, layout, paint of the update
  Note over M: presentation delay
  M->>C: commit frame
  C-->>U: next paint (INP ends here)

parts.label: Fixes and case study
parts.body:
## Code splitting

Shipping less JavaScript up front improves LCP (less competing bandwidth and render-blocking work), INP (less parse, compile and hydration on the main thread) and battery.

| Technique | How | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|
| Route-based splitting | Frameworks do it automatically per page/segment | Shared chunk bloat: one heavy import in a layout ships everywhere |
| Component-level splitting | `React.lazy(() => import('./Chart'))`, `next/dynamic` | Spinners for content above the fold; split below-the-fold or on interaction |
| Interaction-based loading | `import()` inside the click handler (emoji picker, rich editor) | First-use delay; prefetch on hover or idle |
| Vendor hygiene | Replace heavy libraries (moment with date-fns or `Intl`), import per function | Barrel files (`index.ts` re-exporting everything) defeat tree shaking in some setups |
| Server Components | Keep heavy rendering libraries server-side | Accidentally marking a parent `"use client"` |

Measure with a bundle analyser (`@next/bundle-analyzer`, `source-map-explorer`, Vite's `rollup-plugin-visualizer`). Look at what is in the **first-load JS** of your most visited route, not the total.

## Images

Images are the LCP element on most pages.

- **Serve modern formats** (AVIF, WebP) at the right size with `srcset` and `sizes`, so a phone does not download a 2400 px desktop image. `next/image` and image CDNs do this.
- **Never lazy-load the LCP image.** `loading="lazy"` on the hero delays it until layout. Use `fetchpriority="high"` on it instead (`priority` / `preload` in `next/image`).
- **Make it discoverable.** The LCP image should be in the server HTML as a real image element, not set by JavaScript or as a CSS background deep in a stylesheet. If it must be a background, add a preload link.
- **Always set dimensions** (`width`/`height` attributes or CSS `aspect-ratio`) so the browser reserves space and nothing shifts (CLS).
- Lazy-load everything below the fold.

## Fonts

- Self-host or use a framework font loader (`next/font`) to avoid an extra connection to a third-party origin.
- `font-display: swap` (text visible immediately with a fallback) or `optional` (no swap after a short block period, best for CLS).
- Reduce swap shift with **metric overrides** on the fallback (`size-adjust`, `ascent-override`); `next/font` generates these automatically.
- Subset to the scripts you use and preload only the one or two critical font files.

## Third-party scripts

Tag managers, analytics, chat widgets, A/B testing and ads are often the largest source of main-thread work, and you do not control their code.

1. **Inventory and justify** each script with an owner and a business reason. Remove the dead ones (there are always some).
2. **Load late:** after the page is interactive or on interaction (load the chat widget when the user clicks a facade button). In Next.js, `next/script` with `strategy="lazyOnload"` or `afterInteractive`.
3. **Avoid synchronous A/B testing scripts** that hide the page until they run; prefer server-side or edge experiment assignment.
4. **Facades:** a static thumbnail for a YouTube embed that loads the real iframe on click.
5. Consider moving some to a worker (Partytown) only after measuring; compatibility varies.
6. Use `preconnect` for critical third-party origins you cannot avoid.

## Performance budgets and CI

A budget is a number that fails the build when crossed. Without one, performance decays one reasonable-looking PR at a time.

| Budget type | Example | Tool |
|---|---|---|
| Quantity | First-load JS for `/product` <= 170 KB gzip; total images <= 500 KB | `size-limit`, bundler stats, Lighthouse CI `resource-summary` budgets |
| Timing (lab) | Lighthouse LCP <= 2.5 s and TBT <= 200 ms on the mobile profile | Lighthouse CI assertions |
| Rule-based | Lighthouse performance score >= 90 | Lighthouse CI |
| Field | p75 INP <= 200 ms per template, alert on regression | RUM dashboard (`web-vitals` beacons) with alerts |

Make lab checks stable: run Lighthouse 3 to 5 times and take the median, test against a production build, and assert on a few metrics rather than the overall score. Field monitoring catches what CI cannot (real devices, third parties added through a tag manager without a deploy).

## Case study: taking a slow product page to good Core Web Vitals

**Starting point (field p75, mobile):** LCP 4.8 s, INP 420 ms, CLS 0.27. Stack: client-rendered React SPA, 900 KB of JavaScript (gzip), tag manager with 14 tags.

**Step 1: find out where time goes.** CrUX confirms the issue is mobile. RUM attribution shows the LCP element is the hero image; sub-parts: TTFB 0.6 s, **load delay 2.6 s**, load duration 0.9 s, render delay 0.7 s. INP attribution shows the worst interactions are taps on "size" during the first seconds and typing in the search box. CLS source: a promo banner inserted above the gallery, plus a web font swap.

**Step 2: fix LCP load delay (biggest phase).** The hero URL only existed after the JS bundle ran and fetched product JSON. Move the product page to server rendering with the image in the HTML, `fetchpriority="high"`, responsive AVIF via an image CDN. Result in the lab: load delay drops to about 0.1 s.

**Step 3: fix render delay.** Inline critical CSS (the framework handles this), defer non-critical CSS, and remove a synchronous A/B testing script from the head; assign experiments at the edge instead.

**Step 4: reduce JavaScript and hydration.** Bundle analysis shows a charting library and a full icon set in the shared chunk. Lazy-load the size-guide chart on click, import icons individually, and convert static sections (description, specs) to Server Components. First-load JS falls from 900 KB to about 260 KB.

**Step 5: fix INP.** Input delay was hydration and tag-manager work. Delay non-essential tags until after load and interaction; break the product recommendations computation into a worker. For the search box, wrap result-list updates in `startTransition` and virtualise the list. Processing time for the size tap drops because the click handler no longer synchronously recalculates the whole page state.

**Step 6: fix CLS.** Reserve space for the promo banner with a fixed-height slot (or render it server-side), set `aspect-ratio` on gallery images, and use `next/font` with metric-adjusted fallbacks.

**Step 7: lock it in.** Add `size-limit` for the product route chunk, Lighthouse CI assertions on LCP and TBT, and RUM alerts per template on p75 INP.

**Result after the 28-day CrUX window rolls over** (illustrative numbers for a change like this): LCP about 2.1 s, INP about 160 ms, CLS about 0.04. The key lesson is the order: measure in the field, attribute to a phase, fix the biggest phase, verify in the lab, then confirm in the field.

parts.label: Interview
parts.body:
## What interviewers are really testing

Performance questions test **method**, not tips. Interviewers want to see: measure first (field vs lab), break a metric into phases, fix the dominant phase, and prevent regressions. Listing twenty optimisations without a diagnosis is a junior signal; a senior walks from symptom to evidence to fix to guardrail.

## Question 1: "Our LCP is 4.5 s on mobile. What do you do?"

**Model answer:**

> First I confirm it in field data, CrUX or our RUM, and split by device and template, so I am fixing the right page. Then I identify the LCP element and break LCP into its four phases: TTFB, resource load delay, load duration and render delay. Each has different fixes. High TTFB means server or CDN work: caching, fewer redirects, streaming. High load delay usually means the image is discovered late, because it is rendered by JavaScript or lazy-loaded, so I put it in the server HTML with `fetchpriority="high"` and never lazy-load it. High load duration means the file is too big: responsive sizes and AVIF or WebP. High render delay means render-blocking CSS, fonts or client-side rendering. I verify each change in a throttled lab run, then add a budget in CI and watch p75 in the field.

## Question 2: "What is INP and how is it different from FID?"

**Model answer:** INP measures the time from a user interaction (click, tap, key press) until the next frame is painted, across the whole visit, and reports close to the worst one. FID measured only the input delay of the first interaction, so it ignored slow handlers and slow rendering, and most sites passed it. INP has three parts: input delay (the main thread was busy), processing (our handlers), and presentation delay (the rendering work our update caused). Good is 200 ms or less at p75.

## Question 3: "Lighthouse says 98 but users complain the page is sluggish. Why?"

**Model answer:** Lighthouse is one cold load on an emulated device with no interaction, so it cannot measure INP directly; it uses Total Blocking Time as a proxy. Real users interact during hydration, have slower devices, have third-party tags configured in a tag manager that may differ from staging, and spend minutes on the page where slow handlers or memory growth appear. I would look at field INP with attribution (which element, which phase) and LoAF script attribution, then reproduce the slow interaction with a Performance panel recording at 4 to 6x CPU throttling.

## Question 4: "How do you prevent performance regressions across 40 engineers?"

**Model answer:** Make performance a number that fails the build. Bundle budgets per route with `size-limit` or bundler stats on every PR, Lighthouse CI assertions on LCP and TBT against a production build with median-of-several runs, and RUM dashboards with p75 alerts per template for what CI cannot see. Add ownership: each third-party tag has an owner and a review process. Show the bundle diff in the PR comment so the cost of a new dependency is visible before merge.

## Question 5: "A click on a filter takes 600 ms to update a list of 5,000 items. Walk me through fixing it."

**Model answer:**

1. Record the interaction in the Performance panel with CPU throttling and look at the Interactions track and the long task under it.
2. If processing dominates: profile which components re-render. Memoise rows, keep props stable, and filter with a precomputed index rather than re-deriving everything.
3. Render less: virtualise the list so only about 30 rows are in the DOM.
4. Keep the input responsive: update the selected filter chip immediately and wrap the list update in `startTransition` (or `useDeferredValue`) so React can interrupt it.
5. If presentation delay dominates: the DOM change is big or triggers expensive layout; virtualisation and `content-visibility: auto` help.
6. If the filtering itself is heavy (fuzzy search across fields), move it to a Web Worker.
7. Verify the interaction under 200 ms, then add a RUM check on INP for that page.

## Question 6: "How do you fix CLS from a cookie banner and ads?"

**Model answer:** Reserve the space before the content arrives: fixed-size ad slots (with the most common size, accepting some whitespace), and render the cookie banner as an overlay fixed to the bottom so it does not push content, or render it server-side so it is there at first paint. Never insert content above existing content after load unless the user asked for it.

## Quick reference: symptom to fix

| Symptom | Likely cause | First fix |
|---|---|---|
| High TTFB | Slow server data, no caching, redirect chains | Cache at the CDN, stream, parallelise data fetches |
| High LCP load delay | Hero discovered late or lazy-loaded | Server-rendered image element, `fetchpriority="high"`, preload |
| High LCP render delay | Render-blocking CSS, JS, fonts, CSR | Critical CSS, defer scripts, SSR |
| High INP input delay | Long tasks at the wrong time (hydration, tags) | Defer third parties, split code, yield |
| High INP processing | Heavy handlers and re-renders | Memoise, transitions, worker, virtualise |
| CLS | Unsized media, injected banners, font swaps | Dimensions, reserved slots, metric-adjusted fallback fonts |

## Common mistakes

- Optimising the Lighthouse score instead of field p75.
- Lazy-loading the hero image, or adding `preload` for everything (which competes with the resource that matters).
- Assuming a CDN fixes LCP when the LCP image is discovered by client-side JavaScript.
- Forgetting third parties and the tag manager in the analysis.
- Quoting old thresholds or FID as a current Core Web Vital.
- Not mentioning a regression guard; fixes without budgets rot within months.

keyPoints: Core Web Vitals are judged at p75 of real loads: LCP <= 2.5 s, INP <= 200 ms, CLS <= 0.1. INP replaced FID in March 2024.
Break LCP into TTFB, load delay, load duration and render delay; load and render delay should be near zero.
Break INP into input delay, processing and presentation delay; each points to a different fix.
Field data says what is slow; lab tools say why. Lighthouse cannot measure INP and uses TBT as a proxy.
Never lazy-load the LCP image; put it in server HTML with fetchpriority high, correct sizes and modern formats.
Main-thread fixes in order: do less, do it later, break it up, move it to a worker, use transitions.
Third-party scripts are often the biggest INP cost; inventory them, load them late, use facades.
Budgets in CI and RUM alerts keep performance from decaying one PR at a time.

check.q: Field data shows LCP of 4 s with a resource load delay of 2.4 s for the hero image. Which fix targets that phase most directly?
options: Compress the image further
Upgrade the origin server's CPU
Make the image discoverable in the server HTML with fetchpriority="high" and remove lazy loading
Add more CDN regions
check.why: Load delay is time before the browser even starts fetching the image, typically because JavaScript injects it or it is lazy-loaded. Compression shortens load duration, not delay.

check.q: Why can a page score 98 in Lighthouse yet have poor field INP?
options: Lighthouse measures INP on a faster device but otherwise identically
Lighthouse does not interact with the page; it approximates responsiveness with TBT on one cold load
Field INP only counts the first interaction
INP is a desktop-only metric
check.why: INP needs real interactions. Lighthouse loads once without input, so it reports Total Blocking Time as a proxy; real users tap during hydration on slower devices with real third-party tags.

check.q: Which layout shift is excluded from CLS?
options: An ad slot growing after it loads
A web font swap that reflows a paragraph
An image without dimensions pushing content down
An accordion expanding within 500 ms of the user clicking it
check.why: Shifts within 500 ms of a discrete user input are treated as expected and excluded. The others are unexpected shifts that count.
